strengths: Novel and timely problem: First work addressing copyright protection for image knowledge in multimodal RAG systems, filling a critical gap

Well-articulated technical challenges: Clear identification of three unique challenges (indirect propagation, unapparent distribution shifts, explicit retrieval requirement) distinguishing this from text-only RAG watermarking
Simple yet practical solutions: AQUAacronym and AQUAspatial are elegant methods that avoid model retraining and work in black-box settings
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Rigorous testing across 4 VLM models, 2 datasets (~400K+ images), proper statistical hypothesis testing with Welch's t-test, and multiple evaluation dimensions
Strong empirical results: High CGSR (75-99%), superior query efficiency (~30 vs 200+ queries for baselines), robust 0% false positive rate on normal queries, resilience to image transformations
Excellent reproducibility: Public code release, detailed prompts and examples, comprehensive appendices, clear presentation with helpful visualizations
Realistic threat model: Appropriately addresses black-box API-only scenarios reflecting real-world RAG service deployment
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: Restricts to T2T multimodal RAG only, excluding other important architectures (image-to-text, text-to-image, image-to-image RAG). Significantly reduces real-world applicability

Weak baseline comparisons: Naive baseline is strawman-level, Opt. baseline is generic optimization not designed for RAG. Missing critical comparisons with adapted text-based methods (WARD, RAG©). Undermines claims about baseline superiority

Synthetic watermark dependency: All watermarks use LLM-generated captions + diffusion models with limited diversity. Unclear scalability if datasets contain synthetic images. Contradicts 'unapparent distribution shift' claims. No empirical validation of this key assumption

Insufficient adversarial robustness analysis: Only tests basic transformations (rescale 1.5×, 45° rotation, Gaussian blur). Missing JPEG compression, watermark removal attacks, adaptive attacks, and intentional filtering scenarios. No defense mechanism against adversarial actors

Query design and scalability concerns: No systematic methodology for trigger query generation. Requires 50+ watermark images × 10+ probe queries. Unclear scalability for practical deployments and minimum watermarks needed for legal proof

Reference distribution practical impossibility: Real deployment requires pre-computed clean/watermarked reference distributions simultaneously—unrealistic in practice. 'Real-world deployment' strategy (Section 5.3) inadequately addresses this fundamental issue

Limited technical novelty: Methods leverage existing techniques (text embedding + diffusion models). Primary novelty is problem formulation rather than methodological innovation. Straightforward application of standard tools

Incomplete harmlessness evaluation: Only verifies normal queries don't retrieve watermarks, not that watermark images don't degrade RAG performance. High SimScore doesn't guarantee semantic equivalence in actual system behavior

Experimental design limitations: Fixed k=5 retrieval with no sensitivity analysis. No cross-dataset evaluation. Hyperparameters fixed across all experiments without ablation. Limited to QA datasets only

AQUAacronym OCR dependency: Vulnerable to VLM degradation in future models. No evaluation on non-English acronyms or multilingual scenarios. Acronym uniqueness assumption may fail in specialized domains

strengths: Addresses an important and novel problem: copyright protection for image knowledge in multimodal RAG systems, filling a genuine gap in existing watermarking literature
Clearly identifies three unique technical challenges (indirect watermark propagation, unapparent distribution shifts, explicit retrieval requirement) specific to multimodal RAG
Comprehensive experimental framework with two datasets, four VLM variants, multiple evaluation metrics, and assessments across effectiveness, harmlessness, stealthiness, and robustness dimensions
Includes formal statistical rigor with Welch's t-test and hypothesis testing for watermark detection
Well-motivated threat model with realistic defender/adversary roles for RAG-as-a-Service scenarios
Clear presentation with informative figures and logical flow that effectively communicates the problem and approach
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: AQUAacronym amounts to exploiting VLM OCR with embedded text; AQUAspatial uses standard diffusion-based image generation. The core contribution is relatively straightforward with minimal technical depth or innovation

Critical reliance on synthetic/generated images undermines stealthiness claims: synthetic images may be detectable through forensic analysis, lack naturalness, and contradict the claim of seamless integration into real knowledge bases. No evidence provided that they're visually indistinguishable from real images

Insufficient stealthiness evaluation: PCA visualization uses only 5 watermarked samples; no testing against forensic detection methods, anomaly detection, or adversarial filtering mechanisms. Figure 6 shows watermarks remain somewhat separable from natural data

Critical robustness testing gaps: missing evaluations for JPEG/WebP compression, image cropping, brightness/contrast adjustments—transformations more common in practice than the tested rescale/rotate/blur. No cross-model robustness evaluation
Narrow scope limited to T2T multimodal RAG only, excluding image-to-image and other increasingly common architectures. Severely limits contribution scope and relevance

Weak baseline comparisons: Naive baseline is not a meaningful comparison (different approach entirely); Opt. baseline may reflect implementation issues; no comparisons with established image watermarking techniques or alternative watermark injection methods

Practical deployment concerns inadequately addressed: requires 50+ watermark images with 10 query variations each; reference distribution problem means defenders cannot establish ground truth in real deployment (Appendix B offers only example values, not universal guidance); computationally expensive for continuous monitoring

Strong dependency on VLM-specific capabilities: AQUAacronym CGSR varies from 75-99% across models; no strategy for adaptation across VLMs or robustness to future model changes. Cross-model watermark transfer not evaluated

Threat model limitations: assumes defenders can preemptively inject watermarks; doesn't address retrospective protection, different retrievers, fine-tuning attacks, or sophisticated adversarial removal strategies. Assumes 'usable but not visible' policy that may not hold

Methodological issues: exact match verification (Eq. 2) is overly strict without discussing robustness to OCR errors; hypothesis testing assumes normality without validation; SimScore relies on proprietary Gemini model without inter-rater agreement; CGSR conditions on retrieval success masking retrieval failures
Insufficient ablation studies: no justification for acronyms vs. alternatives; no analysis of necessary watermark/query quantities; limited failure case analysis

Reproducibility concerns: relies on proprietary Gemini-2.5-Pro for acronym generation and SimScore computation; uses specific diffusion models whose availability/characteristics may change; reference distributions are example-only and likely not universally applicable
Limited generalization: evaluated only on two QA datasets (MMQA, WebQA); results may not transfer to other multimodal RAG domains (e-commerce, medical imaging, scientific databases)

Missing critical transformations and scenarios: no testing of image compression, cropping, or other common preprocessing; no evaluation against adaptive adversarial attacks or watermark removal; no cross-domain evaluation

Incomplete threat model coverage: doesn't address scenarios where adversaries use different retrievers, perform fine-tuning, mix watermarked images with clean data, or conduct sophisticated detection-through-comparison attacks

strengths: First systematic treatment of copyright protection for image knowledge in multimodal RAG systems, addressing a novel and timely problem

Clear and well-articulated problem formulation that identifies unique challenges (indirect propagation, unapparent distribution shifts, explicit retrieval) distinguishing this from prior watermarking work
Practical and well-designed methodology with two complementary approaches (AQUAacronym and AQUAspatial) that gracefully degrade based on model capabilities
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 VLM generators and 2 datasets with strong empirical results (CGSR 75-99%) and impressive query efficiency (30 vs. 200+ queries)
Thorough multi-faceted assessment covering effectiveness, harmlessness, stealthiness, and robustness, including resistance to common image transformations
Rigorous statistical verification methodology using Welch's t-test and consideration of practical deployment constraints
Good reproducibility with publicly available code and clear experimental setup
Well-written paper with effective visualizations that clearly communicate the problem and solution
weaknesses: Limited scope restricted to T2T Multimodal RAG architecture only; other important configurations (T2I, I2I) are acknowledged but not addressed, limiting generalizability claims
Moderate technical novelty: methods rely on straightforward ideas (embedding text/spatial cues in images) applied to a new setting rather than novel techniques
Weak baseline comparisons with only naive and adversarial perturbation baselines; no comparison to adapted existing methods (WARD, RAG©) or other semantic watermarking approaches
Threat model limitations: assumes adversaries lack knowledge of watermarking scheme and entire database is stolen; no evaluation against adversarial attacks or watermark removal strategies

Stealthiness evaluation concerns: PCA visualization shows clustering of watermark images/queries; claims of undetectability rely on embedding similarity without testing against sophisticated detection methods

Suspicious statistical results with p-values of exactly 0.0 and extremely low values (6.6e-145) suggesting potential oversensitivity; practical feasibility of detection with very low significance levels (3e-5) unclear
Reference distributions in Appendix B are watermark-specific with unclear generalizability across different watermark designs
SimScore metric relies on subjective LLM judgment about semantic similarity without validation or inter-annotator agreement evaluation
Limited theoretical analysis: no capacity bounds, information-theoretic discussion, or formal guarantees; limited analysis of why proposed methods outperform baselines
Scalability not addressed: no evaluation of performance with very large knowledge bases or analysis of computational costs for watermark verification at scale
Watermark quality relies on LLM generation with acknowledged limitation that it 'can only ensure average performance and cannot reach the theoretical upper limit'
Missing ablation studies on key design choices (clip-top-k value, number of watermarks, etc.) and limited analysis of failure modes and model-specific correlations

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem in multimodal RAG systems that existing methods don't cover
Clever technical insight using rare acronyms as watermark carriers that are unlikely to be learned but can be generated
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (MMQA, WebQA) and four VLM architectures with multiple complementary metrics
Strong empirical results showing 78-99% CGSR with 0% false retrieval on benign queries and robustness against image transformations and adversarial attacks
Thoughtful consideration of real-world deployment scenarios including reference distribution estimation and multi-provider collision avoidance
Well-structured paper with clear presentation, detailed appendices, code availability, and reproducibility statements
Systematic evaluation of multiple important properties: effectiveness, harmlessness, stealthiness, and robustness across diverse attack scenarios
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core watermarking techniques (acronyms and spatial configurations) are straightforward applications of existing watermarking principles rather than methodological advances
Weak baseline comparisons using only naive random selection and optimization-based perturbation; missing comparisons to established watermarking frameworks or cryptographic approaches

Incomplete threat model: doesn't adequately address adversaries with knowledge of the watermarking methodology, prompt injection attacks at generator level, or long-term model evolution that could learn to suppress watermarks

Practical scalability concerns: query efficiency requires ~30 queries for statistical significance, proposed centralized registry introduces single point of failure, and scalability with massive image bases not addressed

Statistical methodology issues: no correction for multiple comparisons across models/datasets/attacks, reference distribution estimation assumes unrealistic clean system access, and hypothesis testing approach not clearly justified

Evaluation limitations: all experiments use same watermark methodology (no validation of generalization), limited to two datasets, weak baselines make effectiveness claims less convincing, and cross-domain robustness not thoroughly tested
Query efficiency and practical deployment barriers: 30+ queries needed to achieve statistical significance is potentially impractical for real-world systems

Incomplete adversarial analysis: no discussion of what happens when knowledge base is intentionally poisoned with same acronyms, limited evaluation of semantic-preserving attacks, and concerning utility degradation under adversarial fine-tuning (8.62% loss)

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing an important gap in copyright protection for multimodal RAG systems
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple models (LLaVA-NeXT, InternVL3, Qwen-VL) and datasets (MMQA, WebQA)
Multiple evaluation metrics and thorough robustness testing including image transformations, adversarial attacks, and system-level variations
Extensive supplementary materials with detailed experimental protocols and results across different scenarios
Addresses an emerging problem area with practical implications for RaaS platforms
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core watermarking techniques are straightforward (acronym embedding, spatial cues); lacks innovation in watermarking methodology
Questionable practical effectiveness: watermarks only trigger with highly specific probe queries, making real-world detection unrealistic without access to query design
Weak baselines: no comparison with established watermarking literature; 'Naive' baseline uses random selection; 'Opt' baseline poorly designed compared to robust watermarking methods
Methodological issues: statistical tests assume independence between watermarked images and queries; extremely small p-values (e-182) raise validity concerns; no multiple comparison correction
Insufficient robustness: adversarial fine-tuning reduces CGSR from 99.61% to 87.18% with 8.62% utility degradation; OCR-based filter bypasses watermarks with 2.76% FPR
Incomplete threat model: doesn't address collusion, doesn't explain how verification works when defender cannot design queries, assumes unrealistic knowledge limitations
Limited scope: only evaluated on QA tasks; unclear generalization to retrieval, visual reasoning, or other multimodal applications
Inadequate literature positioning: insufficient comparison with existing watermarking/fingerprinting approaches; unclear why existing methods don't apply
Experimental limitations: only 10 watermark images per method; manually crafted probe queries unrepresentative of natural user behavior; no user studies for imperceptibility validation
Unaddressed practical deployment questions: knowledge base scalability, performance impact, cost of embedding watermarks, handling unintended watermark triggers

strengths: Novel problem addressing a clear gap: First watermarking framework for image knowledge protection in Multimodal RAG systems, which has been understudied while text watermarking is well-explored

Creative and practical solution: Two complementary watermarking strategies (acronym-based and spatial relationships) are intuitive, well-motivated, and address both direct and indirect watermark propagation

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Extensive testing across multiple models (LLaVA-NeXT, InternVL3, Qwen-VL, Qwen2.5-VL), datasets (MMQA 50k, WebQA 389k), and diverse metrics with rigorous statistical validation (Welch's t-test, hypothesis testing)

Strong empirical results: Achieves 85-99%+ CGSR across models with minimal false positives (~0-2%), maintains high retrieval performance, and demonstrates robustness to image-level attacks and system variations

Thorough robustness analysis: Evaluates against image transformations (WAVAD), system-level changes (retriever updates, corpus drift), adversarial fine-tuning, and different parameter scales (2B-38B models)
Practical deployment focus: Addresses real-world challenges including watermark collision mitigation in multi-provider environments, reference distribution estimation, and scalability considerations
Excellent reproducibility: Code released as supplementary material, uses public datasets, provides detailed experimental protocols, hyperparameters, and ablation studies
Clear presentation: Well-written with effective figures, comprehensive appendices with concrete examples (watermark images and probe queries), and visual stealthiness analysis
weaknesses: Weak baseline comparisons: Only compares against naive random selection and simple optimization-based method; missing comparisons with other multimodal watermarking approaches or adaptations of related work (WARD, DMI-RAG)

Scalability concerns: Figure 4a shows sharp degradation in retrieval rate with increasing watermarks; requires N_wm × N_ds queries for verification confidence, which is prohibitive for large-scale RAG systems with millions of images

Incomplete adversarial robustness: Generator-level fine-tuning attacks show degradation (CGSR: 99.61%→87.18%, Utility: 27.25%→24.90%); limited evaluation against sophisticated attacks beyond WAVAD, prompt injection, or alternative retrieval mechanisms

Watermark collision mitigation lacks detail: Proposed solutions (probabilistic mitigation and centralized registry) are not thoroughly evaluated; probabilistic independence assumptions may not hold; centralized coordination complexity underexplored

Limited failure case analysis: Insufficient discussion of when AQUA fails, what query properties complicate detection, or scenarios with naturally-occurring acronyms in images or adversarially-generated content

Watermark visibility concerns: While claiming stealthiness, acronym visibility to human observers not validated; limited visual analysis (Figure 5 could be more extensive); different image types and styles may reveal watermarks differently; no user study on imperceptibility
Narrow scope: Limited to text-to-image RAG paradigm; does not address other multimodal tasks (VQA, image understanding); generalization to future VLM architectures unclear

Simplified theoretical framework: Verification relies on simple substring matching (Equation 2) vulnerable to sophisticated LLM behaviors; no formal guarantees on detection rates or robustness bounds; limited theoretical justification for optimality of proposed strategies

Reference distribution assumptions: Appendix B.1 assumes availability of clean, representative data for distribution estimation; real-world systems may lack sufficient data; statistical power calculations depend heavily on these assumptions

Strong behavioral assumptions: Assumes consistent model behavior, fixed retriever ranking mechanisms, and no model refusal of watermarked queries; generalization to diverse model architectures and training objectives uncertain
